subChunks.title: Access Modifiers

storyBeats.text: Eldrin leads you to the Academy vault. A sign reads: Private — Headmaster access only.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Access modifiers are the locks on your rooms. private means only you may enter. public opens the door to the world. Without locks, any passing apprentice could tamper with your most sensitive artefacts.

storyBeats.label: The locked vault

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice: balance is private. Outsiders cannot set it to -1000. They can only interact through the controlled deposit() method — which validates the amount first.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a class BankAccount with a private double balance. Add a deposit(double amount) method (only deposits positive amounts), a withdraw(double amount) method (only if balance is sufficient), and a getBalance() method. Demonstrate with a deposit of 100, withdrawal of 30, and print the final balance.
guidedPractice.hint: Check amount > 0 in deposit, and balance >= amount in withdraw before modifying the balance.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the four access modifiers in Java. Why is 'private' the recommended choice for class fields?

questions.prompt: Which access modifier makes a field visible only within the class it is declared in?
questions.explanation: private restricts access to the declaring class only — the strictest access level.

questions.prompt: Making a field public is generally considered good practice in Java classes.
questions.explanation: Public fields violate encapsulation — any external code can change them directly, bypassing validation. Fields should be private with access controlled through methods.

subChunks.title: Getters, Setters & Static Members

storyBeats.text: Eldrin shows you two controls on the Academy's power regulator: a dial to read the current level (getter), and a lever to set it (setter) — but the lever has stops preventing dangerously low or high values.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A setter without validation is just a public field in disguise. The point of a setter is to enforce rules. Always ask: what invariants must hold on this data?

storyBeats.label: Validated setter

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Static members are the shared runes of the academy — every wizard reads from the same tome. Use them for counters, constants (static final), and utility methods that don't need any object state.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a Wizard class with: a private static int count, a private String name, a constructor that increments count, and a static getCount() method. Create three Wizards and print the count.
guidedPractice.hint: Increment count++ in the constructor. Access getCount() via Wizard.getCount() (class method, not instance).

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the difference between an instance variable and a static variable in Java? Give an example of when you'd use each.

questions.prompt: A static method in Java can access which of the following directly?
options: Only static fields and other static methods
questions.answer: Only static fields and other static methods
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, not to any instance. They cannot access instance fields or methods without a reference to an object.
The static field n is shared by all instances. Each constructor increments it, so after 3 objects, n equals 3.

questions.prompt: You can override a static method in a subclass in Java.
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, not to instances, so they cannot be overridden — only hidden. Polymorphism does not apply to static methods.
